summary: Describes a framework for using directory services to help edge TRILL switches reduce flooding of unknown-destination frames and ARP/ND traffic, rather than learning only by observing traffic. It is an informational problem statement and high-level design, not a full protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of shouting everywhere to find a person, you look them up in a directory.

questions: reduce unknown unicast flooding in trill
what is the flooding problem in trill data centers
how does directory assistance reduce flooding
push vs pull model for directory
subtitle: Using directories to reduce broadcast flooding in TRILL data centers.

tldr.problem: When TRILL edge switches receive packets for unknown MAC addresses, they flood them across the entire campus. In large data centers with thousands of VMs, this floods cause excessive broadcast traffic and consume switch memory learning MAC addresses that never communicate locally.
tldr.mechanism: A directory service maintains a mapping of MAC addresses and IPs to the TRILL edge switches (RBridges) where they are attached. Edge switches query or receive push notifications from the directory instead of flooding unknown packets, reducing broadcast and improving security.
tldr.outcome: Data center networks using directory-assisted TRILL reduce flooding significantly, lower switch memory consumption, improve security by preventing MAC spoofing, and scale to thousands more endpoints per campus.

facts.label: Data center scale
facts.value: 1,600 server racks, 80,000+ end stations per edge switch

facts.label: Directory entry
facts.value: [IP, MAC, Data Label, attached RBridges, interested RBridges]

today: RFC 7067 is Informational and presents the problem and framework, not the final protocol specification. It has motivated follow-on work to develop actual TRILL directory-assisted protocols. The concepts remain directly applicable to modern data center networks using TRILL or similar switching technologies where broadcast reduction and address management at scale are critical.

sections.title: The Flooding Problem in Large Data Centers
sections.content:
In TRILL networks, when an edge switch (RBridge) receives a packet destined for a MAC address it does not know, it floods the packet across the entire campus to all switches in that VLAN. In traditional networks this is acceptable, but in large data centers with many virtual machines, this behavior causes problems.

Data center networks often have 1,600 or more server racks, each with multiple switches, and each server running multiple VMs. This can result in 80,000+ end stations attached to a single edge switch. When a VM boots up or moves, its ARP (address resolution) and ND (neighbor discovery) traffic gets flooded campus-wide. Switches waste memory learning MAC addresses of remote VMs that may never communicate with local endpoints. The RFC describes this problem and proposes directory-assisted solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: In a data center with thousands of computers and servers, flooding (shouting everywhere) when looking for one computer wastes a lot of network bandwidth and switch memory.

sections.title: What the Directory Knows
sections.content:
A directory service maintains a database with entries containing: an IP address and MAC address pair, a Data Label (VLAN or FGL), the list of edge RBridges where this host is attached, and a list of remote RBridges that might need to know about this host. This structure allows directory servers to proactively notify interested switches about new hosts or updates.

The directory learns this information from the VM management system in the data center (which already knows where VMs are placed and which subnets they belong to) rather than from packet observation. Because data center networks are orchestrated and structured (racks and rows), the information is typically available and can be delivered to TRILL switches efficiently.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory is like a management system that already knows where every computer is, what its address is, and which rack it is in.

sections.title: Two Models: Push and Pull
sections.content:
The RFC describes two operational models for directory-assisted TRILL.

In the Push Model, the directory proactively sends MAC-to-RBridge mappings to edge switches. When a switch boots or when entries change, the directory pushes the relevant data. The advantage is that the switch has all needed information before packets arrive. The disadvantage is that the directory may push more entries than needed, wasting bandwidth and memory.

In the Pull Model, when an edge switch receives a packet with an unknown destination, it queries the directory server before flooding. The directory responds with the target's location or says it does not exist. The advantage is that switches only store frequently used entries; less-used entries age out. The disadvantage is that the first packet to a new destination is delayed while waiting for the directory response.
sections.plainLanguage: Push: The directory sends you updates whenever something changes. Pull: You ask the directory when you need to know something.

sections.title: Benefits and Data Center Deployment
sections.content:
Directory-assisted TRILL offers several concrete benefits: it avoids flooding unknown unicast packets across the campus, reducing unnecessary traffic. It reduces the MAC address learning table size on switches, freeing memory. It prevents unnecessary broadcast and multicast (ARP and ND) from being flooded campus-wide. It also improves security: a spoofed packet with a false source MAC address can be detected if the directory says that MAC should be remote, not local.

These benefits are particularly valuable in data centers where VM migration, rapid workload changes, and server virtualization cause frequent address changes. Data centers have structured topologies (ToR and aggregation switches) and management systems that orchestrate VM placement, making directory information naturally available.
sections.plainLanguage: Less flooding means less wasted network traffic. Smaller switch tables mean cheaper hardware. Fewer spoofed addresses means better security. All of this is especially helpful in data centers where things change quickly.

sections.title: TRILL Campus Boundaries and Scalability
sections.content:
The RFC presents two deployment scenarios for a data center TRILL campus with 1,600 server racks:

Scenario 1: TRILL at ToR (Top-of-Rack) has 1,600+ edge RBridges. This creates a large IS-IS routing area (the network state database that TRILL switches use), putting load on aggregation switches handling hundreds of parallel links. Per-switch MAC tables are manageable (3,200 entries worst case).

Scenario 2: TRILL at Aggregation has fewer than 100 TRILL switches (less routing overhead) but requires each switch to learn up to 320,000 MAC&Label entries. Directory assistance becomes crucial in this scenario: with push or pull directories, switches need not learn entries for remote VMs that never communicate locally.
sections.plainLanguage: Where you place TRILL in the data center network affects how many switches are involved and how many addresses each switch must remember. A directory helps solve this trade-off.

left.title: Push Model
left.desc: Directory proactively sends MAC mappings. Fast response, but may send unused entries.

right.title: Pull Model
right.desc: RBridge queries directory on demand. Smaller tables, but first packet is delayed.
